﻿function Test-MtCisDevicesWithoutCompliancePolicyMarked {
    <#
    .SYNOPSIS
        Checks if devices without a compliance policy assigned are marked "not compliant".

    .DESCRIPTION
        Devices without a compliance policy assigned should be marked "not compliant".
        CIS Microsoft 365 Foundations Benchmark v7.0.0 (4.1, L1)

    .EXAMPLE
        Test-MtCisDevicesWithoutCompliancePolicyMarked

        Returns true if devices without a compliance policy assigned are marked "not compliant".

    .LINK
        https://maester.dev/docs/commands/Test-MtCisDevicesWithoutCompliancePolicyMarked
    #>
    [MaesterTest(
        Id = 'CIS.M365.4.1',
        Title = 'Ensure devices without a compliance policy are marked ''not compliant''',
        Product = 'intune',
        Feature = 'device-compliance',
        Area = 'devices',
        ResourceType = 'Tenant',
        Severity = 'Medium',
        UserImpact = 'Medium',
        ImplementationCost = 'Medium',
        Mitre = 'T1078.004',
        Control = ('cis-m365:4.1', 'nist-800-53-r5:AC-19', 'nist-800-53-r5:CM-6'),
        Service = 'Graph',
        License = 'INTUNE_A',
        Author = 'oed-metzb',
        Contributor = ('Mynster9361', 'Korthal-Maiyn')
    )]
    [CmdletBinding()]
    [OutputType([bool])]
    param()

    Write-Verbose 'Getting settings...'
    $settings = Invoke-MtGraphRequest -RelativeUri "deviceManagement/settings"

    Write-Verbose 'Executing checks'
    $checkSecureByDefault = $settings | Where-Object { $_.secureByDefault -eq $true }

    $testResult = (($checkSecureByDefault | Measure-Object).Count -ge 1)

    if ($testResult) {
        $testResultMarkdown = "Well done. Your tenant settings comply with CIS recommendations.`n`n%TestResult%"
    }
    else {
        $testResultMarkdown = "Your tenant settings do not comply with CIS recommendations.`n`n%TestResult%"
    }

    $resultMd = "| Setting | Result |`n"
    $resultMd += "| --- | --- |`n"

    if ($checkSecureByDefault) {
        $checkSecureByDefaultResult = '✅ Pass'
    }
    else {
        $checkSecureByDefaultResult = '❌ Fail'
    }

    $resultMd += "| Mark devices with no compliance policy assigned as 'Not compliant' | $checkSecureByDefaultResult |`n"
    $testResultMarkdown = $testResultMarkdown -replace '%TestResult%', $resultMd

    Add-MtTestResultDetail -Result $testResultMarkdown
    return $testResult
}
----
﻿4.1 (L1) Ensure devices without a compliance policy are marked 'not compliant'

Compliance policies are sets of rules and conditions that are used to evaluate the configuration of managed devices. These policies can help secure organizational data and resources from devices that don't meet those configuration requirements. Managed devices must satisfy the conditions you set in your policies to be considered compliant by Intune. When combined with Conditional Access, this allows more control over how non-compliant devices are treated.

The recommended state is **Mark devices with no compliance policy assigned as** **Not compliant**

#### Rationale

Implementing this setting is a first step in adopting compliance policies for devices. When used in together with Conditional Access policies the attack surface can be reduced by forcing an action to be taken for non-compliant devices.

>Note: This section does not focus on which compliance policies to use, only that an organization should adopt and enforce them to their needs.

#### Impact

Any devices without a compliance policy will be marked not compliant. Care should be taken to first deploy any new compliance policies with a Conditional Access (CA) policy that is in the Report-only state. After the environment's device compliance is better understood it is then appropriate to finally align with **Mark devices with no compliance policy assigned as** and enable any CA policies that enforce actions based on device compliance.

If a mature environment already has an existing device compliance CA policy and a large number of devices without an assigned compliance policy, this could cause disruption as those devices would then be suddenly considered not compliant.

#### Remediation action

1. Navigate to [Microsoft Intune admin center](https://intune.microsoft.com).
2. Click on **Devices** and then under **Managed devices** on **Compliance**.
3. Click **Compliance settings**.
4. Ensure **Mark devices with no compliance policy assigned as** set to **Not compliant**

##### PowerShell

1. Connect to Microsoft Graph using `Connect-MgGraph -Scopes "DeviceManagementConfiguration.ReadWrite.All"`
2. Run the following commands:

```powershell
$Uri = 'https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/deviceManagement'
$Body = @{
    settings = @{
        secureByDefault = $true
    }
} | ConvertTo-Json
Invoke-MgGraphRequest -Uri $Uri -Method PATCH -Body $Body
```

* [Use compliance policies to set rules for devices you manage with Intune](https://learn.microsoft.com/intune/intune-service/protect/device-compliance-get-started)
* [CIS Microsoft 365 Foundations Benchmark v7.0.0 - Page 184](https://www.cisecurity.org/benchmark/microsoft_365)

`TenantType`, `Cloud`, `Platform`, `Lifecycle`, `LongRunning` and `Exclusive`. Its own are `Id`, `Title`,
  `Control`, `Author`, `Contributor` and its parameters.
- names the requirement it implements first in `Control`, and that requirement is not added to the `Control` of
  the test it calls, so a run reports it once.
- calls a test that is not a shim itself, and passes only parameters that test declares.
- says in its guide what the benchmark asks and links the test it runs by its ID.

`powershell/tests/general/TestShims.Tests.ps1` finds every built-in test whose body is a single `return` of
another built-in test's function and fails when one of these is not true. The result text comes from the test
that is called, so write that test's messages without naming its benchmark.

When the two benchmarks drift apart, change the shim. If the benchmark of the shim asks for something new,
replace the `return` with a test of its own. If the test it calls changes for its own benchmark, check the shims
that call its function and decide for each whether the change applies to its benchmark too.

A Maester test that also checks what a benchmark asks for needs no shim; it names the requirement in its
`Control`, as [Mapping a test to a framework](#mapping-a-test-to-a-framework) describes. A custom test cannot be a
shim, because the functions of built-in tests are not exported; it runs a built-in test with `Invoke-MtTest -Id`
instead (see [What a custom test can call](#what-a-custom-test-can-call)).

## What a benchmark test evaluates

A CIS test does what the benchmark's **PowerShell audit procedure** does: it reads the same objects and passes on
the same condition. The PowerShell steps are the part of an Automated recommendation that can be automated, and
usually its most precise wording. When the UI steps and the PowerShell steps differ, follow the PowerShell steps.

- **Scope.** When the audit reads every object, the test reads every object, including ones that apply to no
  user. CIS 6.2.1 runs `Get-HostedOutboundSpamFilterPolicy` and checks `AutoForwardingMode` on each policy, so
  the test checks custom policies that have no rule. When the audit reads one object, the test reads only that
  one: CIS 2.1.15 runs `Get-HostedOutboundSpamFilterPolicy -Identity Default`, so the test does not evaluate
  custom policies. Don't narrow a test to the policies users receive, or widen it beyond what the audit reads.
  CIS leaves exceptions to the organization, so a test does not decide them for it.
- **Values.** Use the thresholds the audit names or its script sets, such as the 90% of the extension list in
  CIS 2.1.11. When organizations may need a different value, make it a parameter with the benchmark's value as
  its default.
- **Missing data.** When the object the audit reads is not returned, the test fails or reports an error. It never
  passes because there was nothing to check.

A view of the policies users actually receive belongs in a Maester (MT) test, not in a benchmark test. The same
rule applies to CISA tests, with the SCuBA baseline and ScubaGear's policy in place of the CIS audit procedure.

    Checks that an assigned Intune policy sets the attack surface reduction rule "Block Office applications from injecting code into other processes" to Block.

    Attack surface reduction rules are read from every Intune Windows configuration policy (Endpoint security
    and settings catalog share the setting definition IDs). The check passes when an assigned policy sets the
    rule to Block; Audit and Warn only report the behaviour and do not satisfy the control.

        Title = 'Microsoft Office is blocked from injecting code into other processes.',
        Product = 'intune',
        RelatedProduct = 'defender',
        Feature = 'endpoint-security',

        ResourceType = 'Tenant',
        Severity = 'High',

        Service = 'Graph',
        License = 'INTUNE_A',

    )]

﻿Microsoft Office is blocked from injecting code into other processes (ISM-1669, Essential Eight Maturity Level Two, User application hardening).

Injecting code into another process lets a macro hide its activity behind a trusted program and evade controls that watch Office. No legitimate document needs it. This check reads the attack surface reduction rules of every Intune Windows configuration policy (Endpoint security and settings catalog policies share the same setting definitions) and passes when an assigned policy sets **Block Office applications from injecting code into other processes** to **Block**. Audit and Warn only report the behaviour and do not satisfy the control.

#### Remediation action

1. In **Microsoft Intune admin center**, go to **Endpoint security** > **[Attack surface reduction](https://intune.microsoft.com/#view/Microsoft_Intune_Workflows/SecurityManagementMenu/~/asr)** and open your attack surface reduction rules policy, or create one for **Windows** with the profile **Attack Surface Reduction Rules**.
2. Set **Block Office applications from injecting code into other processes** to **Block**. Pilot the rule in **Audit** first if Office add-ins or line-of-business macros are in use.
3. Assign the policy to all workstations.

﻿function Test-MtAsdSmartLockoutThreshold {
    <#
    .SYNOPSIS
    Checks that the Microsoft Entra smart lockout threshold is five failed sign-ins or fewer.

    .DESCRIPTION
    ISM-1403 (Guidelines for system access, User account lockouts) asks that user accounts, except for break
    glass accounts, are protected by fixed or risk-based lockout mechanisms aligned to a maximum of five failed
    logon attempts. This control is not part of the Essential Eight maturity model. The ASD Blueprint for Secure
    Cloud sets the smart lockout threshold to 5.

    CIS.M365.5.2.3.8 reads the same setting and allows up to 10, so this test runs that check
    (Test-MtCisSmartLockoutThreshold) with ASD's maximum. The Microsoft default of 10 fails.

    .EXAMPLE
    Test-MtAsdSmartLockoutThreshold

    Returns true when the smart lockout threshold is 5 or fewer.

    .LINK
    https://maester.dev/docs/tests/ASD.ISM-1403
    #>
    [MaesterTest(
        Id = 'ASD.ISM-1403',
        Title = 'User accounts are protected by lockout mechanisms aligned to a maximum of five failed logon attempts.',
        Product = 'entra',
        Feature = 'password-protection',
        Area = 'authentication',
        ResourceType = 'Tenant',
        Severity = 'Medium',
        UserImpact = 'Low',
        ImplementationCost = 'Low',
        Mitre = ('T1110.001', 'T1110.003'),
        Control = ('ism:ISM-1403', 'nist-800-53-r5:AC-7'),
        Service = 'Graph',
        Author = 'jusso-dev'
    )]
    [CmdletBinding()]
    [OutputType([bool])]
    param(
        # The most failed sign-ins allowed before an account is locked. ASD sets five; CIS allows ten.
        [ValidateRange(1, 50)]
        [int] $MaximumLockoutThreshold = 5
    )

    return Test-MtCisSmartLockoutThreshold -MaximumLockoutThreshold $MaximumLockoutThreshold
}
----
﻿User accounts, except for break glass accounts, are protected by fixed or risk-based lockout mechanisms aligned to a maximum of five failed logon attempts, with either indefinite or automated lockout durations (ISM-1403, Guidelines for system access).

Online password guessing is cheap: an attacker who can try ten passwords per account before a lockout gets ten chances at every account in the tenant. Microsoft Entra smart lockout counts failed sign-ins per account, locks the account for the lockout duration when the threshold is reached, and counts familiar and unfamiliar locations separately so that a user at their usual desk is not locked out by an attacker elsewhere.

This test runs the same check as [CIS.M365.5.2.3.8](https://maester.dev/docs/tests/CIS.M365.5.2.3.8) with ASD's maximum: the lockout threshold must be 5 or fewer (the `MaximumLockoutThreshold` parameter), where CIS allows 10. The Microsoft default of 10 fails. The ASD Blueprint for Secure Cloud sets a threshold of 5 and a lockout duration of 60 seconds.

#### Remediation action

1. In the [Microsoft Entra admin center](https://entra.microsoft.com), go to **Entra ID** > **[Authentication methods](https://entra.microsoft.com/#view/Microsoft_AAD_IAM/AuthenticationMethodsMenuBlade/~/PasswordProtection)** > **Password protection**.
2. Set **Lockout threshold** to **5** and **Lockout duration in seconds** to at least **60**.
3. Select **Save**.

#### Related links

* [ISM Guidelines for system access: User account lockouts](https://www.cyber.gov.au/business-government/asds-cyber-security-frameworks/ism/cyber-security-guidelines/guidelines-system-access)
* [ASD Blueprint for Secure Cloud: Password protection](https://blueprint.asd.gov.au/configuration/entra-id/protection/authentication-methods/password-protection/)
* [Protect user accounts from attacks with Microsoft Entra smart lockout](https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/identity/authentication/howto-password-smart-lockout)

compliant' (Automated)
Profile Applicability:

Description:
Compliance policies are sets of rules and conditions that are used to evaluate the
configuration of managed devices. These policies can help secure organizational data
and resources from devices that don't meet those configuration requirements. Managed
devices must satisfy the conditions you set in your policies to be considered compliant
by Intune. When combined with conditional access, this allows more control over how

as as Not compliant
Rationale:
Implementing this setting is a first step in adopting compliance policies for devices.
When used together with Conditional Access policies the attack surface can be reduced
by forcing an action to be taken for non-compliant devices.
Note: This section does not focus on which compliance policies to use, only that an
organization should adopt and enforce them to their needs.
Impact:
Any devices without a compliance policy will be marked not compliant. Care should be
taken to first deploy any new compliance policies with a Conditional Access (CA) policy
that is in the Report-only state. After the environment's device compliance is better
understood it is then appropriate to finally align with Mark devices with no
compliance policy assigned as and enable any CA policies that enforce actions
based on device compliance.
If a mature environment already has an existing device compliance CA policy and a
large number of devices without an assigned compliance policy, this could cause
disruption as those devices would then be suddenly considered not compliant.

## 📑 Description

CIS.M365.4.1 now runs MT.1054's check instead of a copy of it: its body is `return Test-MtDeviceComplianceSettings`. It follows "Reviewing a test for duplicates" in `AGENTS.md`.

**Why it's a duplicate.** The CIS Microsoft 365 Foundations Benchmark v7.0.0, 4.1 (p.185), audits with `GET https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/deviceManagement/settings` and verifies that `secureByDefault` is `True`. MT.1054 reads the same property and passes only when it is `true`, so both tests checked the same setting in two different ways. MT.1054 reads the beta endpoint, which returns the same property. When the setting isn't returned, the test still fails.

**What changes**

- `tests/cis/Test.CIS.M365.4.1.ps1`: the body is now the one `return`. The test keeps its own `Id`, `Title`, `Control` (`cis-m365:4.1` first) and guide. Its other attributes already matched MT.1054's. The help now says which test it runs, and `.LINK` points to the test page, as CIS 4.2 does.
- `tests/cis/Test.CIS.M365.4.1.md`: one paragraph that names [MT.1054](https://maester.dev/docs/tests/MT.1054) and explains what the audit checks.
- The result text now comes from MT.1054, which doesn't name a benchmark, as the writing-tests guide asks. The old "comply with CIS recommendations" wording and its one-row table are gone.

- This isn't a bug fix, so under the 3.0 code freeze it can wait until after the release.
